title: Doubt was only partial, never universal
source_text: XXXVI. Secundo vero dico, nullorum librorum, qui vere divini sint, authoritatem unquam ita fuisse dubiam, ut omnes & passim de iis dubitarint. Sed dubitatio illa quorundam tantum fuit: apud reliquos vero eorum fuit certa authoritas. Ita verum est quidem Epistolam ad Hebraeos, Epistolam Jacobi, & Joannis Apocalypsin, quibusdam fuisse suspectas, & a quibusdam habitas pro supposititiis: attamen apud plerasque Ecclesias authoritatem suam semper obtinuerunt. Nec ullum tempus assignari potest quo non in magna orbis Christiani parte receptae fuerint, & pro divinis & authenticis habitae. Quod indicant ipsa loca quae referunt adversarii tanquam suae causae faventia. Ita negantibus Arianis authoritatem Epistolae ad Hebraeos respondet Theodoretus, Oportebat eos, si non aliud, certe diuturnitatem temporis revereri, quo hanc Epistolam in Ecclesiis perpetuo legerant veritatis alumni. Et sic Apocalypsin adversus Marcionem tuetur Tertullianus, Habemus & Joannis alumnas Ecclesias, nam etsi Apocalypsin ejus Marcion respuit, ordo tamen Episcoporum ad originem recensitus in Joannem stabit authorem. Quod vero spectat Epistolam Jacobi, idem ille Eusebius qui dicit illam quibusdam videri νόθον, adulterinam esse, testatus eam in quamplurimis Ecclesiis fuisse publice receptam.
pass_a_gloss: But second I say that the authority of no books which are truly divine ever was so doubtful that all men everywhere doubted concerning them. But that doubt was only of certain persons: among the rest their authority was certain. Thus it is indeed true that the Epistle to the Hebrews, the Epistle of James, and John's Apocalypse were suspect to some, and by some held as spurious: yet among most Churches they always obtained their authority. Nor can any time be assigned in which they were not received in a great part of the Christian world and held as divine and authentic. Which the very places the adversaries cite as favoring their cause indicate. Thus to the Arians denying the authority of the Epistle to the Hebrews Theodoret answers, They ought, if nothing else, certainly to reverence the long duration of time in which the pupils of the truth had continually read this Epistle in the Churches. And so Tertullian defends the Apocalypse against Marcion, We have also John's foster-churches, for although Marcion rejects his Apocalypse, yet the order of bishops recounted to the origin will stand firm in John as author. But as for the Epistle of James, that same Eusebius who says it seemed to some to be νόθον, spurious, testified that it had been publicly received in very many Churches.
pass_b_english: Second: no truly divine book's authority was ever so doubtful that everyone everywhere doubted it. The doubt belonged only to some; among the rest their authority stayed certain.

Hebrews, James, and John's Apocalypse were indeed suspect to some, and by some treated as spurious — yet among most churches they always kept their authority. No time can be named when they were not received in a large part of the Christian world and held divine and authentic.

The very passages the adversaries quote as favoring them show this. Against Arians who denied Hebrews, Theodoret says they ought at least to reverence the long stretch of time in which the truth's pupils had continually read that epistle in the churches.

So Tertullian defends the Apocalypse against Marcion: we also have John's foster-churches; though Marcion rejects his Apocalypse, the line of bishops traced back to the origin will still stand on John as author.
As for James, the same Eusebius who says some thought it νόθον — spurious — also testifies that it was publicly received in very many churches.
